extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and olympiad-level mathematics students; self-learners in linear algebra
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter introducing inner products, norms, orthogonality, Hilbert spaces, Gram–Schmidt, and basic Fourier analysis, with definitions, theorems, examples, and problems aimed at building conceptual and problem-solving mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real inner form (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let V be a real vector space. A real inner form ⟨•, •⟩ : V × V → R which satisfies: symmetry (⟨v,w⟩ = ⟨w,v⟩), bilinearity (linear in each argument; e.g. ⟨cx+y,z⟩ = c⟨x,z⟩+⟨y,z⟩), and positive definiteness (⟨v,v⟩ ≥ 0 with equality iff v = 0V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise notes that linearity in the first argument plus symmetry implies linearity in the second, so one could require only ⟨−,v⟩ linear. Example: standard dot product on R^n with basis e_i; positive definiteness shown by sum of squares. Use original wording: 'positive definite nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form' as an alternative name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex inner product (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let V be a complex vector space. A complex inner product ⟨•, •⟩ : V × V → C which satisfies: conjugate symmetry (⟨v,w⟩ = ⟨w,v⟩̄), sesquilinearity (linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear/anti-linear in the second), and positive definiteness (⟨v,v⟩ ∈ R_{2}0 and equals 0 iff v = 0V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit linearity: ⟨cx+y,v⟩ = c⟨x,v⟩+⟨y,v⟩; anti-linearity: ⟨v,cx+y⟩ = c̄⟨v,x⟩+⟨v,y⟩. Remark explains necessity of conjugate symmetry: without it bilinear forms on complex spaces can fail to give real ⟨v,v⟩ (example with ie). Example: standard dot product on C^n with conjugation on second factor; Exercise: check the standard C^n form is a complex inner form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner product space (conceptual requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inner product space is either a real vector space with a real inner form or a complex vector space with a complex inner form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linear maps between inner product spaces are not required to be compatible with the inner form unless specified. This allows uniform treatment of real and complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norm from inner product (definition and properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an inner product space V, the norm is defined by ∥v∥ = sqrt(⟨v,v⟩). This yields a metric d(v,w)=∥v−w∥, satisfying d(v,w)=0 iff v=w and the triangle inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangle inequality is proved via Cauchy–Schwarz; examples: Euclidean norm on R^n or C^n. Emphasized that positive definiteness ensures the square root is well-defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (statement and equality condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any v,w in an inner product space, |⟨v,w⟩| ≤ ∥v∥ ∥w∥, with equality iff v and w are linearly dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof method: consider ⟨cv−w,cv−w⟩ ≥ 0 and choose c = (∥w∥/∥v∥)·(|⟨v,w⟩|/⟨v,w⟩) to force desired inequality. Equality case analyzed via this construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality (statement and equality condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any v,w we have ∥v∥ + ∥w∥ ≥ ∥v + w∥, with equality iff v and w are linearly dependent and point in the same direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested proof: square both sides and apply Cauchy–Schwarz. This is the key step to make the inner-product-induced norm into a metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonality (definition and consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two nonzero vectors v and w are orthogonal iff ⟨v,w⟩ = 0. Any set of pairwise orthogonal nonzero vectors is linearly independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of independence: take a linear dependence and inner-product with one of the vectors to isolate its coefficient. Use this to motivate stronger basis notions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthonormal basis (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An orthonormal basis of a finite-dimensional inner product space V is a basis e_1,...,e_n such that ∥e_i∥ = 1 for every i and ⟨e_i,e_j⟩ = 0 for i ≠ j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: standard basis of R^n/C^n. Theorem (Gram–Schmidt) guarantees existence in finite dimensions. Once an orthonormal basis is chosen, inner products reduce to coordinate dot-products: ⟨∑a_i e_i, ∑b_i e_i⟩ = ∑ a_i b_i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection operator (formula and use in Gram–Schmidt)
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonzero u, define proju(v) = ⟨v,u⟩/⟨u,u⟩ · u. Gram–Schmidt constructs an orthonormal basis by recursively subtracting projections: u1=e1, u2=e2−proju1(e2), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction yields pairwise orthogonal nonzero u_i; normalizing gives orthonormal basis. Use this explicit algorithm to produce orthonormal bases from any basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of inner product in orthonormal coordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any finite-dimensional inner product space and an orthonormal basis e_i, the inner product can be written as the coordinate dot product: ⟨∑a_i e_i, ∑b_i e_i⟩ = ∑ a_i b_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains ubiquity of the dot product and shows that choice of orthonormal basis identifies V with R^n/C^n with the standard inner product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert space (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hilbert space is an inner product space whose metric space is complete (every Cauchy sequence converges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This completeness permits meaningful infinite linear combinations and limits. Finite-dimensional inner product spaces are automatically Hilbert spaces (Problem 13B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence criterion for orthogonal series in Hilbert spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an orthonormal sequence e_i and scalars c_i, the partial sums v_n = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i e_i converge in the Hilbert space iff ∑ |c_i|^2 < ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: convergence iff sequence of partial sums is Cauchy, and ∥v_j−v_i∥^2 equals tail sum of |c_k|^2; completeness of R implies equivalence with boundedness/convergence of the series of squares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthonormal basis in Hilbert space (infinite case definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An orthonormal basis for a Hilbert space V is a (possibly infinite) sequence e_1,e_2,... with ⟨e_i,e_j⟩ = δ_{ij} and every v∈V can be expressed uniquely as v = ∑ c_i e_i with ∑ |c_i|^2 < ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes finite orthonormal bases and enforces l^2 condition to ensure convergence of expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier decomposition framework (abstract requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a domain Z, equip the complex vector space of functions f:Z→C with a positive definite inner product (typically an average or integral). Select an orthonormal basis (characters) e_ξ; then every f decomposes as f(x) = ∑_ξ b_f(ξ) e_ξ with coefficients b_f(ξ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: characters (frequencies) are chosen to be symmetric/nice functions (sines, cosines, exponentials, multilinear polynomials). This is the conceptual framework behind all subsequent Fourier results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary Fourier analysis (orthonormal basis and coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Z={±1}^n with inner product ⟨f,g⟩=(1/2^n)∑_{x∈Z} f(x) g(x), the multilinear polynomials χ_S(x)=∏_{i∈S} x_i form an orthonormal basis. Fourier decomposition: f = ∑_{S⊆{1,...,n}} b_f(S) χ_S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise: show orthonormality and that b_f(∅) equals average value (1/|Z|)∑ f(x). For ±1-valued functions, ⟨f,f⟩=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier on finite abelian groups (characters and prerequisites)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite abelian group Z, define inner product ⟨f,g⟩=(1/|Z|)∑ f(x) g(x). Choose a symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form ·: Z×Z→T satisfying bilinearity, symmetry, and nondegeneracy; characters e_ξ(x)=e(ξ·x) form an orthonormal basis indexed by ξ∈Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Z/nZ with ξ·x = ξx/n. Proof of orthonormality uses summation identities. Choice of · is largely harmless (different choices give equivalent bases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier series on L^2([−π,π]) (classical basis and function space)
rubrics_metrics.description: L^2([−π,π]) := {f: [−π,π]→C : ∫ |f(x)|^2 dx < ∞}, modulo almost-everywhere equality, with inner product ⟨f,g⟩=(1/2π)∫ f(x) g(x) dx. The family e_n(x)=exp(inx) (n∈Z) is an orthonormal basis and any f has Fourier series f(x)=∑_{n∈Z} b_f(n) exp(inx) (with ∑ |b_f(n)|^2 < ∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: L^2 is infinite-dimensional Hilbert space; one often assumes periodic boundary f(−π)=f(π) to view f as function on T. Coefficients given by b_f(n)=(1/2π)∫ f(x) exp(−inx) dx.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parseval/Plancherel/Inverse Fourier (identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the orthonormal-basis/Fourier context: (1) Parseval: ∑_ξ |b_f(ξ)|^2 = ⟨f,f⟩ (sum or integral depending on domain). (2) Fourier inversion: b_f(ξ) = (1/|Z|)∑_{x∈Z} f(x) e_ξ(x) (or analogous integral for L^2). (3) Plancherel: ⟨f,g⟩ = ∑_ξ b_f(ξ) b_g(ξ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These follow from general facts about orthonormal bases: coefficients are inner products with basis vectors; use to compute norms, inner products, and reconstruct functions. Exercises show concrete computations (e.g., bf(∅)= average).

rubrics_metrics.name: Roots-of-unity / discrete transform technique (application guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Z/nZ with characters e_{ξ}(x)=e(ξx/n), one can use roots-of-unity filters to extract periodic sums: e.g., reconstructing sums with period 3 using coefficients and evaluating expressions like ∑ binomial coefficients times roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided with cube roots of unity (ω) and decomposing a function f on Z/3Z into three frequency components; compute sums by combining Fourier coefficients with geometric factors (1+ω^k)^{1000} etc. Useful as computational trick in combinatorics/number theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier-based combinatorial/probabilistic arguments (use in proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourier coefficients and Parseval can be used to translate combinatorial/probabilistic constraints into algebraic inequalities on coefficients (e.g., in proof of Arrow's theorem, express probability of paradox as 1/4 plus a sum over S of expressions involving |S| and products of Fourier coefficients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: express probabilities in terms of Fourier coefficients, apply inequalities like |ab+bc+ca|≤a^2+b^2+c^2 and Parseval to deduce support restrictions on coefficients, leading to structural conclusions (e.g., dictatorship). Example: Theorem 14.7.1 proof sketch.
